message.content: Explain in 15 short numbered lines how a scrollbar works.

content.text:
1. A scrollbar is a control that shows which part of a longer document is visible.
2. The track is the full length of the scrollable area.
3. The thumb is the draggable piece inside the track.
4. Its size is the visible area divided by the total content height.
5. A large thumb means little content is hidden; a small one means a lot is.
6. Its position is the scroll offset divided by the scrollable range.
7. Dragging the thumb changes the scroll offset.
8. Clicking the track jumps one screen-height up or down.
9. Arrow buttons at each end scroll by a small fixed step.
10. The mouse wheel and trackpad send scroll events that change the same offset.
11. The app redraws only the lines that fall inside the new window.
12. The thumb is recalculated whenever the content or window size changes.
13. When content fits the window, the scrollbar is hidden or disabled.
14. Terminals keep a scrollback buffer of past lines so the bar has something to scroll through.
15. Scrolling changes which slice of that buffer is drawn, not the buffer itself.

message.content: Write one long paragraph of about 120 words about terminals, no line breaks.

content.text: A terminal is one of the oldest and most durable ways to talk to a computer. It began as a physical keyboard and screen wired to a mainframe, and it still exists today as a small window that accepts text commands and prints text back. Every line you type is read by a shell, which parses it, runs the named program, and streams the output back into the same window. Because the interface is plain text, terminals are fast, scriptable, and easy to automate, which is why developers rely on them for everything from building software to managing servers. Modern terminal apps add tabs, colour, scrollback buffers, and GPU rendering, but the core idea has not changed: you type, the machine answers, and the conversation continues line by line.
